overview:
Slovakia is a small, mountainous country in the heart of Europe, landlocked between Poland, Ukraine, Hungary, Austria and the Czech Republic. It covers about 49,000 km², a little larger than Denmark, and roughly 5.4 million people live there. The Danube River forms part of the southern border and flows through the capital, Bratislava, which sits so close to its neighbors that a cyclist can reach two other countries in an afternoon.

Slovak is the national language, so close to Czech that most Slovaks understand it without ever studying it. Slovakia is a parliamentary republic, a member of the European Union, and it uses the euro. Car factories are its biggest industry; Slovakia builds more cars for each person living there than any other country. Beyond the factory towns the landscape is one of forested hills, ruined castles perched on rocky crags, spa towns, and wooden churches built without a single iron nail.
landAndNature: The Carpathian Mountains sweep across northern Slovakia, and their highest range, the High Tatras, throws up bare granite peaks; Gerlachovský štít reaches 2,655 meters. Below them lie glacial lakes called tarns and deep valleys where brown bears, wolves, lynx and chamois still live, giving Slovakia one of Europe's largest bear populations. Limestone underlies much of the country, dissolved by water into more than 7,000 known caves, several open to visitors. The Dobšiná Ice Cave keeps its ice all year round. Rivers such as the Váh and Hron run south into the fertile Danube lowland, where white storks build enormous nests on chimneys and poles each summer.
peopleAndCulture: Slovak folk traditions are living habits rather than museum pieces: embroidered costumes, painted village houses like those at Čičmany, and the fujara, a shepherd's flute nearly two meters long that is played standing up and is protected by UNESCO. Hearty food suits cold winters, and the national dish is bryndzové halušky, potato dumplings with sheep cheese and bacon. Ice hockey empties the streets when the national team plays; Slovakia won the world championship in 2002. Hiking and skiing fill weekends in the Tatras. At Easter, boys in some villages still sprinkle girls with water for good health, and Christmas brings carp, sauerkraut soup and wafers with honey.
history: Slavic peoples settled the region in the 500s, and in the 800s the empire of Great Moravia spread Christianity here using a new Slavic alphabet brought by the monks Cyril and Methodius. For roughly a thousand years the land belonged to the Kingdom of Hungary, and Bratislava, then called Pressburg, served as the Hungarian capital and coronation city. After World War I, Slovaks joined Czechs in the new state of Czechoslovakia. It was broken apart during World War II, then governed by a communist party from 1948 until the peaceful Velvet Revolution of 1989. On January 1, 1993, Czechoslovakia divided calmly in two, and Slovakia became an independent country without a shot being fired.
funFacts: Slovakia builds more cars per person than any other country, with giant factories turning out around a million vehicles a year.
Bratislava is the only national capital in the world that borders two other countries, Austria and Hungary.
Eleven Hungarian kings and several queens were crowned in Bratislava's St. Martin's Cathedral between 1563 and 1830.
Slovakia's embassies have long swapped misdelivered mail with Slovenia's, because letters are so often sent to the wrong country.
Slovakia has more than 180 castles and hundreds of smaller manor houses, one of the highest numbers per person anywhere.
